entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16974"/><div sID="gen33549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16974"/>3. The Corinthian women, on the ground of the abolition of distinction of sexes in Christ, claimed equality with the male sex, and, overstepping the bounds of propriety, came forward to pray and prophesy without the customary head-covering of females. The Gospel, doubtless, did raise women from the degradation in which they had been sunk, especially in the East. Yet, while on a level with males as to the offer of, and standing in grace (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>), their subjection in point of order, modesty, and seemliness, is to be maintained. Paul reproves here their unseemliness as to dress: in <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, as to the retiring modesty in public which becomes them. "The woman is of the essence of the man, and not made by the man; so, too, the Son is not made by the Father, but of the essence of the Father" [Theodoret, t. 3, p. 171]. <div eID="gen33553" type="x-p"/>

It was the Greek custom (and so that at Corinth) for men in worship to be uncovered; whereas the Jews wore the Talith, or veil, to show reverence before God, and their unworthiness to look on Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Is 6:2</reference>); however, Maimonides [Mishna] excepts cases where (as in Greece) the custom of the place was different.<div eID="gen33556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dishonoureth his head--</hi>not as Alford, "Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1Co 11:3</reference>); but literally, as "his head" is used in the beginning of the verse. He dishonoreth his head (the principal part of the body) by wearing a covering or veil, which is a mark of subjection, and which makes him look downwards instead of upwards to his Spiritual Head, Christ, to whom alone he owes subjection. Why, then, ought not man to wear the covering in token of his subjection to Christ, as the woman wears it in token of her subjection to man? "Because Christ is not seen: the man is seen; so the covering of him who is under Christ is not seen; of her who is under the man, is seen" [Bengel]. (Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.7">1Co 11:7</reference>). <div eID="gen33557" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16976"/><div sID="gen33558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16976"/><hi type="bold">5. woman ... prayeth ... prophesieth--</hi>This instance of women speaking in public worship is an extraordinary case, and justified only by the miraculous gifts which such women possessed as their credentials; for instance, Anna the prophetess and Priscilla (so <reference osisRef="Acts.2.18">Ac 2:18</reference>). The ordinary rule to them is: silence in public (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). Mental receptivity and activity in family life are recognized in Christianity, as most accordant with the destiny of woman. This passage does not necessarily sanction women speaking in public, even though possessing miraculous gifts; but simply records what took place at Corinth, without expressing an opinion on it, reserving the censure of it till <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">35</reference>. Even those women endowed with prophecy were designed to exercise their gift, rather in other times and places, than the public congregation.<div eID="gen33558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dishonoureth ... head--</hi>in that she acts against the divine ordinance and the modest propriety that becomes her: in putting away the veil, she puts away the badge of her subjection to man, which is her true "honor"; for through him it connects her with Christ, the head of the man. Moreover, as the head-covering was the emblem of maiden modesty before man (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.65">Ge 24:65</reference>), and conjugal chastity (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Ge 20:16</reference>); so, to uncover the head indicated withdrawal from the power of the husband, whence a suspected wife had her head uncovered by the priest (<reference osisRef="Num.5.18">Nu 5:18</reference>). Alford takes "her head" to be man, her symbolical, not her literal head; but as it is literal in the former clause, it must be so in the latter one.<div eID="gen33559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all one as if ... shaven--</hi>As woman's hair is given her by nature, as her covering (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.15">1Co 11:15</reference>), to cut it off like a man, all admit, would be indecorous: therefore, to put away the head-covering, too, like a man, would be similarly indecorous. It is natural to her to have long hair for her covering: she ought, therefore, to add the other (the wearing of a head-covering) to show that she does of her own will that which nature itself teaches she ought to do, in token of her subjection to man. <div eID="gen33560" type="x-p"/>

Man is declared in Scripture to be both the "image," and in the "likeness," of God (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.3.9">Jas 3:9</reference>). But "image" alone is applied to the Son of God (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). "Express image," Greek, "the impress." The Divine Son is not merely "like" God, He is God of God, "being of one substance (essence) with the Father."
